strengths: Well-motivated problem: Compelling empirical evidence (Fig. 3) that null-space-based isolation fails under correlated task distributions, addressing real limitations in prior LoRA-based CL methods
Solid theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.1 elegantly connects LoRA capacity to feature projection energy with exact closed-form solutions (Theorems 3.2-3.3) rather than approximations

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive benchmarks across 5 datasets with multiple settings (5S/10S/20S), 20+ baselines, multiple backbones (ViT, CLIP, DINO, iBOT), and model sizes, with consistent improvements of 0.8-1.7% ALast without replay
Practical efficiency: Zero extra parameters at inference, task-count-independent storage (27MB for ViT-B/16), with transparent overhead analysis and no need for storing past-task models

Thorough analysis: Effective ablation studies clearly demonstrating each component's contribution, loss landscape visualizations validating the approach, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis with multiple design choices explored
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Individual components are incremental (projection energy is intuitive but not fundamentally new; GAO adapts existing gradient-alignment ideas; closed-form recalibration applies standard optimization), with contribution primarily in their integration rather than novel concepts

Theory-practice gaps: Theorem 3.1 derived for single gradient step while practice uses many iterations; Theorem B.4 relies on strong assumptions (local linearity, cone decomposition) with limited empirical validation; no analysis of behavior under feature distribution shift

Unjustified design choices: No ablation for why E_old + E_new (not alternatives) defines general subspace; relative energy ratio (E_new/E_old) is heuristic without justification; hyperparameter sensitivity (w_G, λ, ρ_max) requires dataset-specific tuning per Fig. 8
Modest improvements on easier benchmarks: CIFAR100 (0.27% improvement with overlapping error bars), CUB (0.04%, essentially tied), suggesting benefits may be dataset-dependent rather than universal

Limited failure mode analysis: No discussion of failure scenarios, task ordering sensitivity, or extreme task distributions; only 3 random seeds (modern standard is 5-10); statistical significance tests not reported despite claiming superiority; recalibration assumptions not empirically validated
